title: Realtime threading priority & CPU governor impact on decode tail latency across A100/H100/L40S
body:
Purpose:
This is an experiment log and informal write-up exploring how OS-level scheduling (real-time pthread priorities/SCHED_RR) and CPU governor settings (performance vs ondemand) affect decode latency and tail behavior for small-batch, low-latency LLM inference across three representative GPU classes (NVIDIA A100, H100, L40S) on different cloud SKUs and driver/CUDA stacks. The goal is to find low-risk operational knobs we can apply in Dedicated and Private deployments to reduce p99 without regressing throughput/cost materially.

Motivation / context:
We often see persistent sub-100ms p50 and noisy p99 spikes for short responses (batch=1, seq~32-128) even when GPU decode looks healthy. Investigation hypothesis: some portion of tail events are caused by CPU-side interference — thread preemption, kernel-launch jitter, interrupt handling, and CPU frequency scaling — rather than purely GPU kernel performance. Prior notes in the labbook focused on kernel-launch fanout and PCIe locality; this doc looks at scheduler and governor-level knobs that are easy to apply at the host level.

Test matrix:
- GPUs / SKUs: A100 (cloud sku: gc-a100-highmem-1), H100 (aws p5.xlarge analog), L40S (azure NCas_T4_v3 style) — instances chosen to match memory / PCIe vs NVLink topologies we use in Dedicated clusters.
- Driver / CUDA: driver 525.85 + CUDA 11.8, driver 535.x + CUDA 12.1, driver 555.x + CUDA 12.2 (where available on the cloud sku).
- OS knobs: CPU governor = performance vs ondemand; scheduling policy for decode/stream management threads = SCHED_OTHER (default) vs SCHED_RR @ priority 10 vs pinned affinity to isolated cores.
- Workloads: small-batch text-gen decode microbenchmarks using a trimmed-serving-runtime harness: batch=1, temperature sampling disabled, seq_in=32, seq_out=48; also test seq_out=512 for medium-length. Tests run for 2k decodes per configuration, with periodic KV-cold resets (clear model KV cache and warm 1 request every 5 minutes) to surface repopulation spikes.
- Telemetry: per-request p50/p90/p99 latency, CPU usage (per-core), context-switch rate (perf sched_switch), IRQ counts, kernel launch timing (runtime instrumentation), and GPU kernel durations as baseline.

Procedure notes:
1) Boot instance with monitoring agent and perf pinned. Ensure hyperthreading state is consistent across SKUs.
2) Run baseline with default OS config and driver version X. Collect 2k requests.
3) Toggle CPU governor and re-run.
4) Toggle thread scheduling to SCHED_RR for the main decode thread and pin to isolated core(s). Re-run.
5) Cross-check on other driver versions.
6) Repeat for H100 and L40S SKUs.

High-level results (summary):
- p50 behavior: largely unaffected by scheduler changes on all SKUs; p50 determined mostly by GPU kernel execution time and queue latency.
- p99 behavior: improved substantially on A100 and L40S when running decode/stream threads as SCHED_RR on isolated cores with CPU governor=performance. Typical reductions: A100 p99 ~ -20 to -35% (absolute from ~340ms -> ~230ms for short seq), L40S p99 ~ -15 to -28%. H100 saw smaller improvements, occasionally small regressions for some driver combos.
- jitter tradeoff: SCHED_RR reduced long tails but introduced more short-term variance for non-isolated workloads when we did not pin interrupts off those cores. When IRQ affinity overlapped decode cores, p99 worsened.
- driver dependence: driver 535.x + CUDA12.1 generally had the best kernel-launch consistency on L40S; driver 525 setups on A100 showed larger context-switch coupling to kernel-launch latency. On H100, the newer driver (555.x) improved absolute decode times but increased sensitivity to CPU governor (i.e., ondemand introduced larger tails).

Representative numbers (short seq, batch=1) — aggregated approximations from runs: 
- A100 / driver 525 / ondemand / SCHED_OTHER: p50=62ms, p99=345ms
- A100 / driver 525 / performance / SCHED_RR(p10) pinned: p50=60ms, p99=220ms
- H100 / driver 555 / performance / SCHED_RR(p10) pinned: p50=40ms, p99=120ms (but some runs: p99 spiking to 190ms if IRQ affinity not moved)
- L40S / driver 535 / performance / SCHED_RR(p10) pinned: p50=75ms, p99=250ms -> pinned + IRQ isolation: p99=180ms
(Notes: absolute numbers are from microbench harness with trimmed model and network disabled; do not conflate with production API numbers.)

Observations and interpretive notes:
- Why does SCHED_RR help? The decode path includes a tight loop on CPU orchestrating GPU kernel launches, memory copies, and stream callbacks. Preemption of that thread between small kernel launches amplifies per-token latency jitter. Elevating priority and isolating core(s) reduces those preemption windows.
- Governor matters for short bursts. Ondemand/ondemand-like governors can delay CPU frequency ramp-up on the first few kernel-launch-heavy cycles, causing a small-amplitude tail; performance keeps clocks high and reduces that effect. The impact magnitude varies across CPU families underlying the cloud SKU—some instances have aggressive P-states that exacerbate tail.
- H100 less sensitive to these knobs for p99 in many configurations because absolute GPU kernel time dominates; but H100 can still exhibit system-level spikes when interrupts or host-side GC (e.g., Python GC) coincide with kernel launch sequences.
- IRQ and kernel threads must be coordinated. If decode threads run on isolated cores but system IRQs are left on the same cores, p99 gets worse. Always set irqbalance / smpaffinity or explicit irqpinning with decode core isolation.

Operational recommendations (low-risk first):
1) For Dedicated deployments where we control the host: ship a host profile that sets CPU governor=\"performance\" on nodes serving low-latency workloads plus a systemd slice for \"serving-runtime\" with RealtimePriority=10 and CPUAffinity to a small core pool. Adjust IRQ affinity to avoid overlap.
2) For Private/VPC installs: provide an ops-runbook with the above knobs and a small agent check that validates irq/cpu isolation and reports p99 regression.
3) For Hosted API: be conservative. Rollouts with SCHED_RR require kernel capability and careful tuning; recommend pilot on a small Dedicated fleet first. If we can afford host-level changes in a dedicated offering, enable by default.
4) Driver advice: prefer driver 535+CUDA12 for L40S families in our testing; pin driver versions per region and bake into SKU compatibility matrix.

Known limitations and caveats:
- These tests were microbench-only, trimmed model, and without multi-tenant noise. In multi-tenant nodes shared with other user workloads, SCHED_RR priority can starve background tasks and impact density. Evaluate density tradeoffs before enabling across fleets.
- Results vary by CPU generation and cloud provider host firmware. Treat absolute numbers as heuristics.
- Real-time scheduling requires CAP_SYS_NICE or similar host privileges; not suitable for unprivileged containers without additional host config.

Next steps / experiments to run:
- Repeat the most promising config (A100 + performance + SCHED_RR + IRQ isolation) under realistic multi-tenant injection noise (background docker processes, network bursts) to validate cost/density tradeoffs.
- Test combined with our auto-batching code path and streaming decode loop to quantify any interactors with batching coalescing windows.
- Automate a small telemetry probe that runs a 200-request microbench on new drivers/firmware changes to detect regressions.

Quick action items:
- Create a small PR to add a host profile template and systemd slice example for ops (assigned: @Liam).
- Raise a pilot ticket to enable governor=performance + SCHED_RR on a 3-node Dedicated pool in staging (JIRA-ENG-2143).
- Add a CI job to run microbench on driver upgrades (owner: Marco).

Appendix: commands / snippets used (notes)
- Set policy and pin thread (example from harness):
  pthread_setschedparam(decode_tid, SCHED_RR, { .sched_priority = 10 });
  sched_setaffinity(0, cpuset_for_isolated_cores);
- Set governor:
  for c in /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu[0-9]*; do echo performance > $c/cpufreq/scaling_governor; done
- IRQ pinning:
  echo 2 > /proc/irq/<irq_num>/smp_affinity_list  # move network IRQs off decode cores
- Perf probes collected: perf record -e sched:sched_switch -c 1 -a -g -- sleep 120

Raw logs and perf traces are attached in the experiment folder in the labbook (see linked_artifacts).
